newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian president blasts bank on inflation.
newsitem.headline: Colombian president blasts bank on inflation.

text.p: President Ernesto Samper accused Colombia's Central Bank of not playing its part in reining in the "peverse taxi meter" of rising consumer prices, forced up by inflation and the strengthening peso, in a televised speech Monday.

Inflation for the year to date is running at 18.43 percent, outstripping the annual forecast of 17 percent. This coupled with a strengthening peso has driven up the cost of goods to consumers and has undermined the peso value of export earnings.

Despite the steady slide of the dollar of late, the Central Bank has not stepped in to devalue the peso, arguing that it has not yet reached the floor of the permitted intervention band and is hoping that a strong peso will help stem inflation.

"The way to cut inflation is not to take more money out of the consumers pocket or follow the type of tactics used by the Central Bank which is just watching the peso revalue...we will pressure the Central Bank to contribute its share and stop this peverse taxi meter of the peso revaluation," Samper said in his weekly TV broadcast to the nation.
In addition to his populist sideswipe at the technocrats of the Central Bank, Samper also launched a broadside on private schools for raising tuition fees by what he said was 53 percent.
He also admitted, however, that the price of some public services had recently risen by as much as 30 percent and urged the nation to pull together to tackle the problem of spiraling prices.

"Just because some sectors get out of line doesn't mean that everybody has to break ranks. We must join together and that way we can still have an inflation figure close to what was forecast," he said.
One mechanism Samper singled out as being a valuable tool in controlling prices was the so-called Social Pact -- an agreement between both sides of industry to regulate price rises.
